utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Petrovic, or is it Mr. Rodic has something to raise? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I wished, before the evidence continues, to address you with regard to a particular problem. On Friday, when we finished our work, at the very end, at my intervention, you notified the witness that he was not supposed to communicate with anyone until his evidence continued and was brought to an end ultimately. However, the lawyers, Mr. and Mrs. Nikolic, on Friday visited Admiral Jokic. That is one matter I wish to raise. Secondly, during the last three days of the examination-in-chief, although it was said that the presence of the lawyers in the courtroom was only a matter of courtesy, during every break during our working hours, there was communication, brief communication in all fairness, but nevertheless communication between the witness and his lawyers. That is to say, during every break. Also, there was communication during these breaks between the lawyers and our learned friends of the Prosecution. I believe that in this way the evidence is being compromised, the testimony given by Witness Jokic. That was the objection I wished to raise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, we take issue with communication about the case. Exchange of pleasantries, I think, is never banned. And my understanding of the admonition that is given to witnesses with regard to communication, the sequestration, the order to sequester, is that they are never to discuss the case with anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They are precisely the words I used on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That is my understanding in virtually every Chamber of the Tribunal. And so, I'm sorry, but I believe this is unfounded. And I -- it would help if the Chamber understands that in all manner and means his -- your admonition of course is respected. At least insofar as my understanding of what the admonition is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for bringing the matter to our attention, Mr. Rodic. The position of the accused is that he may not discuss his evidence in this case with anyone else. He may speak to you. He may speak to his own lawyer. He may speak to court officers. He may speak to the Prosecutors on other matters. I'm sure as his counsel is present in the Chamber he will have heard what has been said. He will understand that the evidence being given by his client is not to be discussed while his client is in the course of his evidence. And perhaps I could mention that frequent and unnecessary contact between them will only excite the sort of concern that you have expressed. But at the moment, I think the Chamber can proceed on the basis indicated by Ms. Somers, that there may have been social chat or just personal reassurance or other matters that may have been discussed. We will accept the position that the direction given by the Chamber has been observed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I address you just briefly. I understand what you're saying, if these are brief contacts during the workday, during the breaks, for a few minutes, to walk up to the witness, et cetera. However, on Friday, it was a two-hour visit. So I do have justified doubts as to the purpose of that visit. I cannot believe that it was only the family or the weather that were discussed over two hours. And especially in this situation, when such important evidence is being given. That is one problem. And the other one, I wish to say is the following: We're working in a very small courtroom, but we have Admiral Jokic's lawyer sitting very close to us. So it is very hard for us, the Defence counsel, to discuss things amongst ourselves, and also to discuss things with the accused since the witness's lawyer is sitting so close to us. So could that please be redressed as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's quite possible, given the recent events that have affected the affairs of the witness, that there may have been reason for a lengthy interview with his lawyers about other matters. So we'll leave that where it is for the moment. We can't change anything that is past. But I think we have made it very clear that there should not be discussion of the evidence as the case continues. I have just looked around the courtroom. I don't see where else it is possible to sit. I'm afraid you will just have to be discreet in your conversations between each other. I'm sorry about that, but we have no control over the fact that this week we must be in this very small courtroom. In the other courtrooms, alternative arrangements are possible. But as you can see, it's pretty much a full house. Almost every seat in the house is taken as it is. Now, Ms. Somers, are you ready for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. We are, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have Admiral Jokic in, please. Could we have the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Admiral. May I remind you of the affirmation you took at the commencement of your evidence, which still applies. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Somers: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Admiral Jokic. I would ask all parties, all persons to please turn their attention to a document which has been supplementarily placed before all of you. It is -- I don't believe it is assigned a number. But it is the agreement for cease-fire of 7 December 1991. And it should be on your Sanction screens, and I believe it has been distributed as well, if it will assist. If you just take a very brief look at it, and then I will move on very quickly. Admiral Jokic, do you see before you a document which at the end of it bears your name and has a date of 7 December 1991, 1530 hours at Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this document also the agreement that is signed by Ministers Davorin Rudolf, Ivan Cifric, and Petar Kriste of the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a cease-fire agreement, Admiral, that was negotiated on the 5th of December and was to have been brought into full implementation on the 6th of December following a morning meeting with the parties who have signed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Admiral, just by way of asking you which particular provision may have been the one that required a little looking after. If you could take a look at Article 3, please if it's on your copy, Article 3 which is in English on the second page. Do you see it, Admiral? Is it there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't got it here on the monitor. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It isn't on the monitor, okay. Perhaps a hard copy might be helpful, if that's... Okay. Do you see it now, Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Article 3 the control of traffic? Is this the particular --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have the Serbo-Croatian version? Okay, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now I do, yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can just comment, is Article 3 the provision that needed some additional consideration as of the 5th, but otherwise it was the only article that -- I'm sorry. It was otherwise a cease-fire that you understood to be implemented right away?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely because of this Article 3, on the 5th of December, the agreement was not initialled because we could not agree where the ships would be checked, at sea or in Gruz harbour. And then it all became clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And other than this provision everything else was understood to be effectively a done deal as of the 5th?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask to move this document in evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Two things --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May I first have a correction made in the transcript of my remarks earlier on page 2, line 10. I think I may have said, "The accused." I meant, "The witness." If that could be corrected. Now, Mr. Rodic, you have a submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted to mention something. This agreement, among the other documents contained in the binder, it was included when Witness Hvalkov Pero testified. Will it remain within that single number it was assigned then? Are we going to give it another number? How are we going to deal with it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very good question, Mr. Rodic. Ms. Somers, are you wanting to tender it twice?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. We had checked yesterday, and it didn't come back as having been tendered. So if we're in error, if it is tendered -- okay. In which case, my apologies. It just didn't show up in our search. So I simply would ask, no need to have it retendered. It's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can we be reminded of the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It appears P61. Thank you very much to counsel for bringing that to our attention. We weren't able to confirm it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, I wanted to move along at a rapid rate. I want to just remind you where we left off on Friday. My last question to you before we broke was -- my last two, so you have a context. "Speaking about the morning of the 6th, are we speaking about the same date. Did you on the morning of the 6th when this attack on the Old Town took place, did you issue after you learned about the attack an order not to attack the Old Town?" Your answer was: "Absolutely, yes." My next question was: "Did General Strugar issue that morning an order not to attack the Old Town?" Your answer was: "I don't know. I mean in his order, in his written order and the decision to order operations, that's the name of the document, that was written on the evening of the 5th or the 6th, and it was valid for the 6th. His organs wrote that what is prohibited is the opening of fire starting from 1200 hours on the 6th of December. That is what it says quite literally in that order. As for the other orders of his, I mean, I don't know."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Strugar ask as to -- when it became known that there was, in fact, an attack on the Old Town, did he ask what was going on, or did he not indicate or did he indicate that whatever was going on as to Old Town needed to be stopped? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is what I know: General Strugar called me and told me that General Kadijevic had called him, and he said that he was very angry, furious because Dubrovnik was being attacked. This came as a major surprise to me. I was practically in shock. How was this possible? How did he know? Who informed him, et cetera? What did he mean, Dubrovnik. I just know that at 6.00 my --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but my question to you, if you can just give it a brief answer since we are really under time constraints, is did General Strugar ask what was going on, or did he in some way say to you or to any subordinate that you know of that whatever was happening to the Old Town that morning needed to be stopped? That is my question to you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that Captain Kozaric informed you that Captain Kovacevic requested artillery fire, or support. What artillery in terms of calibre did he request from Captain Kozaric? And what formation did that artillery belong to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked for support from my artillery for support, 130-millimetre guns and 105-millimetre howitzers. I beg your pardon, I stand corrected. 130 millimetres and 85 millimetres. Those that belonged to my command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you allow them to be given to Captain Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I gave strict orders that not a single shell should be fired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say, "My artillery," are you referring to sector artillery?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was it located?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was located in the area of the Cilipi airport runway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have stated that you instructed Captain Kozaric to find the captain of the battleship, Zec, and Colonel Kovacevic. At any stage during this time did you succeed in contacting Captain Zec? If so, how?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not contact any one of them. I ordered him to find them and to send them both to Zarkovica. Actually, the Zec should call me first, and Kovacevic, he should send him immediately to Zarkovica in order to stop the attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was Zec at the time when you made the request to find him? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in his apartment. That is what I was told. His apartment in Herceg Novi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Captain Zec call you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think he called me from Kupari, from Kozaric, because we could not get any contact with Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you tell him to do?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I ordered him to go to the observation post immediately, to the commander of the 3rd Battalion, to stop the attack immediately and to return the unit to its initial position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that observation post?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was at the Zarkovica feature. That was the observation post of the commander of the 3rd Battalion, Captain Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you succeed in contacting Colonel Kovacevic? If so, how, where?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Colonel Kovacevic when I went to Cavtat in the meantime, in order to talk to the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik. I met him in his vehicle on the way. I stopped him, and I ordered him, too, to go to Zarkovica to see Captain Kovacevic and to stop the attack. If he could not do so, he should replace Captain Kovacevic. He should remove him from his duty. He should remove him from his command position, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "Him," to whom are you referring? You say, "Remove him." Whom do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant Colonel Kovacevic because he was my assistant commander for land forces. And he was in this area [as interpreted] all the time, and his task was to control the work of Captain Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. When you say he should remove him, remove who?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we just have to clarify the transcript. I'm sorry for interrupting. The witness said that Colonel Kovacevic was all the time in that battalion. And in the transcript, it says, "In that area." So the difference is significant. What I'm referring to is on page 10, line 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I just reask the question. I think it might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Admiral, for any confusion, but let's start again. My question to you after you said -- I said did you succeed in contacting Colonel Kovacevic? If so how, where? Answer, I met Colonel Kovacevic when I went to Cavtat. I met him in his vehicle on the way, I stopped him, and I ordered him if he could not -- I'm sorry, ordered him, too, to go to Zarkovica to see Captain Kovacevic and to stop the attack. If he could not do so, he should replace Captain Kovacevic. He should remove him from his duty. He shall remove him from his command position, that is. Then my question do you is when you say, "Him," "Remove him," to whom are you referring? And I'll go to the next point that Mr. Petrovic asks about. "Remove him," who is the him?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that Colonel Kovacevic should replace the commander of the 3rd Battalion, Captain Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. Now, the next point is -- let's see, sorry. Okay. You -- you originally answered: "I meant Colonel Kovacevic because he was my assistant commander for land forces, and he was in this area all the time and his task was to control the work of Captain Kovacevic." Would you please indicate what Colonel Kovacevic's assignment was? Did you mean "area"? I think you heard Mr. Petrovic's question. Perhaps you could clarify what you meant by where Colonel Kovacevic was all the time.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not mention "area" at all. I just said that Colonel Kovacevic, as my assistant for the land forces, was in charge of that unit, the 3rd Battalion, of the Trebinje Brigade. And also for Captain Kovacevic, he was supposed to monitor his work and to assist him in his command. And that is what he did all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying, Admiral. What other steps did you take to stop the attack? Did you send any other officers up to the area? Besides Captain Zec and Colonel Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the meantime, I made contact on the telephone, before I left Kumbor. I spoke to Gojko Djurasic, Major Gojko Djurasic, who was commander of Mokosica. He asked me to deal with something. And in that telephone conversation, I told him to go to Zarkovica urgently and help to stop this attack. He was a very good officer. Also, I spoke to Captain Kozaric on the phone, and I told him, since he didn't have any connection with Zarkovica, I told him to call the command post in Brgat and to order the deputy commander of the battalion, Captain Soldo to go to the observation point in Zarkovica and to convey a message to the battalion commander to stop the attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you are able to give approximate times, when did you dispatch Captain Zec to Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. It could have been between 8.00 and 9.00, around half past 8.00. As soon as I got in touch with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you dispatch, if you recall, approximate time is okay, Colonel Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime later. First Zec reported to me while I was still in Kumbor. And for the lieutenant colonel, I met him on the road to Cavtat. That was a bit later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about Colonel Djurasic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure of that. Most probably later, maybe even after 10.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you confirm that all the officers you just spoke of actually got to Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received reports from Kozaric, because I did not have communication with Zarkovica. He was the one who confirmed to me that both of them had gone there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, the three officers whom you sent up there were part of the 9th VPS. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us or do you know if the second operational group command sent any officer to stop the attack?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have such information. I only know that General Grubac who did not belong to the 2nd Operations Group or the 9th sector at the time was in Kupari. And immediately after that, he went to Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is Grubac?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Grubac was sent from the General Staff to monitor combat operations and to report on that with a view of writing an expert report or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the officers on Zarkovica have any success in stopping Captain Kovacevic immediately?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't manage to stop him. It took quite a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given any explanation as to why not, why they were not effecting your order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 10.00 or half past 10.00, when I had already spoken with Dubrovnik twice, I heard a very short report from my deputy Zec. He told me that it was very difficult for him to withdraw his units because of the losses that Kovacevic had suffered and that -- for that reason it was very difficult for him to withdraw because Kovacevic's units had come under fire from the city of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened in the interim period between the time you dispatched these officers and the time that fire ultimately ceased? Do you know what was going on up in Zarkovica? Were you getting any types of reports?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Zec reported to me once and told me that withdrawal was very difficult, that Kovacevic was suffering losses, that there was a lot of casualties, a lot of wounded and dead, and that he was endeavouring to stop the attack as soon as possible. The order that I issued was that at 11.00, all the artillery fire should stop because I had made such an arrangement with the citizens of Dubrovnik. And the fire did indeed stop around half past 11.00. I was on my way to the Cilipi airport, and I was to fly from there by helicopter to Podgorica. However, once I left Dubrovnik, fire continued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So despite your attempts to have a cease-fire, there was fire beyond the point of 11.00, 11.30?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give to the best of your understanding or at least what you were able to learn when fire ceased?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that according to information that I have, this was after 2.00. And according to the information that we received from Dubrovnik, this happened around 1400 hours or 1430. I believe that the truth is somewhere in the middle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So continued at least from 5.45 in the morning until mid or perhaps -- if you're not sure -- but at least mid-afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it lasted between 6.00 in the morning and the early hours of the afternoon, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you returned -- when you returned from your journey to Belgrade, was there still fire going on?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time did you return?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 1730 I was in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do in response to General Strugar's telephone message regarding General Kadijevic's instructions?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did everything possible in order to stop the attack. I called the Crisis Staff in Dubrovnik to explain that I wasn't the one who had ordered the attack, that it was a decision made by my inferior commander. And I also tried to establish the situation and see who it was who issued an -- the order for the attack and how the attack had started in the first place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was thinking more -- I was -- perhaps I wasn't clear. But logistically, what did you do to get yourself to see General Kadijevic? Can you tell us, did you meet General Strugar? Did you go individually? How did you get to Belgrade? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Strugar gave me the message. He told me what General Kadijevic had ordered him. Whenever I did all it took to stop the attack, I was to be prepared to go to Podgorica and then to join him on his way to Belgrade, to the General Staff where the two of us were to report about this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 15 -- page 15, line 16, in the transcript, it says, "He told me what Kadijevic had ordered to him." And the Admiral said, "He told me what Kadijevic had ordered me to do."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I reask the question so we can get clarification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, you heard Mr. Petrovic's comment. Perhaps you can revisit the question and clarify for us. The question was did you go individually? How did you go to Belgrade? Your answer as read is: "General Strugar gave me the message. He told me what General Kadijevic had ordered him." What should your answer be?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is the correct interpretation. He ordered him to tell me. After 13 years, it is very difficult to remember every word. But this is the essence. General Kadijevic ordered General Strugar for the two of us to come to Belgrade to report to him. And that is the essence of my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was my next question. And the order, as you understood it, was for both you and General Strugar to report to General Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this stage -- well, excuse me. Let me just... How did you travel to Podgorica?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By helicopter from Cilipi airport. This is near Cavtat. I was there. I conducted negotiations with the people from Dubrovnik. I arrived at the airport near Podgorica. General Strugar was already there. I was about half an hour late.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which would have put you at what time approximately?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was around 1.00 when we took off for Belgrade. It was around 1300 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this stage, how did you feel, how did you as a person and as a commander feel about the shelling of the Old Town and the imminent meeting with General Kadijevic, particularly in the context of the pending cease-fire and the instructions which General Kadijevic gave on December 3rd to keep the troops under control?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was very concerned. I was still in a state of shock. And all this time, while travelling to Belgrade, I was so concerned that I did not even speak to General Strugar. We did not engage in any meaningful conversation at all. All this time, I was telling him how this was possible? Where did he muster the courage from to attack Srdj? At that time, I still didn't know the extent of damage in the town of Dubrovnik, and I was all the time asking myself questions as to how this had been possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To clarify something you just said, please --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To clarify something you just said. You said: All this time I was telling him how was this possible? Where did he muster the courage to attack? When you say, "He," who do you mean? "He muster the courage."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to Captain Kovacevic all this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say, "I was telling him," who are you referring to when you were telling him?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- from the conversation, if you're able to, or from just the general atmosphere during your travel, did it appear to you that General Strugar knew about the shelling of the Old Town? And if so, did he seem worried?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not as worried as I was, of course, because my responsibility was more direct. He comforted me, and he told me that General Kadijevic wouldn't do anything to me, that he couldn't do anything to me, that all this would pass, that he probably responded to the provocation of the Croats from Srdj. And the damage was not that great. And all such things along these lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "Because my responsibility was more direct," what did you mean by that? Can you explain that.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that battalion was under my direct command. I was its immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was General Strugar the commander over all the battalions, over all the formations, including the one that is the offending formation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, could you have ordered such an attack outside of General Strugar's order? Could you have done that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, of course not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say -- let me just get the -- excuse me one second. I'll get the phrase. When you indicated that he told you, he, I guess -- by "he," whom do you mean? You said: "He comforted me, and he told me General Kadijevic wouldn't do anything to me, that he wouldn't do anything to me, that it would all pass." What did you mean "he"? Who is he?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to General Strugar because there were just the two of us engaged in that conversation, in that dialogue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The two of you are going to Belgrade to meet the -- with General Kadijevic. Now, General Strugar is going there as your commander?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you surprised by this attitude of General Strugar's, considering the orders prohibiting the attacks on the Old Town, as well as the orders relating to the imminent cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what to say. At that time, I was so preoccupied with my own worries that I didn't pay too much attention to that. It somehow did not come home. The comforting words that he said to me when he said that Kadijevic wouldn't do anything to me just didn't reach me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you was did it surprise you that he was saying that in light of all the circumstances and what you were feeling?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one may say so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What in particular were you concerned about? Why -- excuse me, I'll wait for a second. Why were you -- what were you actually concerned about when meeting General Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that a battalion commander under my command who had been ordered not to open fire still carried out such a wilful attack, even after the agreement had been reached. I was worried as how this would all end up because there was a possibility that I would be removed. I was going to resign myself anyway, but I was concerned that this would come across as - how shall I put it - those circumstances were of such a kind that were unpleasant for any soldier. So what I'm talking about is me being removed from my duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you think that as your commander General Strugar should have had the same concerns?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think about that. He was not so concerned. He knew more than me because he was directly subordinated to the General Staff and Kadijevic. So he was better informed about the relationships and how things were done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now what do you think? Do you think that he should have been concerned?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you concerned that General Kadijevic would get a picture of the real condition of the command in the 2nd Operational Group at all levels and its failings?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I presented my situation very sincerely as far as that case was concerned, the attack of the battalion on Srdj and what arose and what transpired after that, the attacks on town afterwards and so on and so Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. forth. And I also spoke about the command, but I didn't speak about the 2nd Operational Group. I didn't have the right to speak about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the meeting with General Kadijevic held and who was present?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was at the General Staff, and in addition to General Kadijevic there was also the Chief of Staff, General Blagoje Adzic, and the chief of the operational administration, General Simonovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened at that meeting in Belgrade? What was General Kadijevic's response to the shelling of the Old Town and the attack in general?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Kadijevic was very angry. All this time, he was pacing around his office. He couldn't sit down. He was very sick at the time. I saw him for the first time after the beginning of October. He kept on attacking us, both of us, General Strugar and myself. When he spoke to us, he addressed us in plurals, so I believe that he referred to both of us. And he said, "I ordered you not to approach Dubrovnik and get within the range of their cannons. They provoked you. You didn't react wisely. You allowed yourself to be provoked into this and to open fire. You did not react wisely," and so on and so forth. "You know that they tend to exaggerate every reaction, every provocation of ours. You know that the representatives of the European Union are on their side. There has been a lot of -- there was an outcry about this attack in the international community. And we have to make sure that this is resolved in the best possible way." This is the essence of the words that he said to us at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you consider as you were hearing these words the fact that you yourself after the shellings in November, which were directed against the Old Town, did you not agree that the weaponry should have been -- did you not agree that they should have removed the weaponry, you should have removed it from the proximity of Dubrovnik, that it in and of itself placed an additional danger in the hands of a particular battalion?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I agreed with General Kadijevic's word in myself. However, I was very sorry that I didn't know what he had ordered. I didn't receive his orders. So this did not refer to me. All of his orders, the orders of the General Staff, went to the command of the 2nd Operational Group. And I received these orders from other people. So I was not aware of the exact ideas of the General Staff about the blockade. Does it have to be a strict blockade? I was not aware of the real operational goals. And I was very sorry that my commander, General Strugar, didn't ask the floor. He did not talk. Everything was addressed to me. Kadijevic actually spoke to both of us using the second person plural. But I was the only one who spoke at that meeting. Nobody else but me asked the floor at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So whom was he addressing concerning the orders, then? Was he addressing General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I have been saying all along, he kept saying, "I ordered you," you in the second person plural. And I kept wondering to myself how could I be included when I never received orders from the General Staff and General Kadijevic. But that is what he kept saying, "I ordered you." He must have meant General Strugar, but he wasn't direct. I don't know why he didn't actually say it, who it was that he gave these orders to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You earlier - or just a few moments ago - said you didn't have the right to speak about the 2nd Operational Group. Why not? Or speak for the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because in the Yugoslav People's Army, a command is far more centralised than perhaps in other armies. Before the chief of General Staff, or rather the minister of defence I cannot criticise the work of my Superior Command at such a meeting. That's at least what my view about this was. If this were an investigation, though, if direct questions were put in this regard, then perhaps. But for me to speak up, to be the first to speak about this, I thought I didn't have the right to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your superior commander was at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My superior commander was General Strugar. I thought that he was the one who should proffer an explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Strugar proffer any explanation at that particular meeting with General Kadijevic, General Adzic, and General Simonovic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He did not ask for the floor at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was General Kadijevic's response with regard to Captain Kovacevic? What did he say about Captain Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked me who this man was, how it was possible that he should undertake such an attack. I gave him an answer by way of the remarks I made, that I did not know him, that I first met him on the 10th of November when that battalion was resubordinated to me, and that is when this attack was launched, that this was a capable, young brave officer, but it seems that his braveness was of the crazy type. But at that time, I did not know him. He had assumed duty from his seriously wounded commander, and that he certainly was not up to the level required for leading such a unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "Of the crazy type," are you suggesting recklessness, or what are you suggesting by that term?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean all of it put together, especially later on when I investigated all of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What casualties did Captain Kovacevic's battalion take as a result of his attacking on the 6th?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, he had 5 dead and 14 wounded. But otherwise, that battalion had sustained their greatest casualties, more than the entire brigade together in the totality of these operations. So this shows this crazy braveness of his and recklessness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Strugar know about the recklessness of Captain Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he thought about him. But I do know that he looked up to him as an officer. In his opinion, he was an ideal officer in terms of all of his characteristics and also in the opinion of others at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "He looked up to him," are you saying General Strugar looked up to Captain Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell General Kadijevic that you had proposed the withdrawal of the 472nd Brigade earlier in time following concerns about discipline?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. For the most part, I said things by way of an answer to what he had asked. But for a while, I gave a free interpretation of what was going on around the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you feel about General Strugar's silence in the face of the criticism being expressed by General Kadijevic and leaving you to do the explaining?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was very hurt on account of that because I realised that I was left out in the open on my own, and that General Strugar did not want to explain more extensively how this happened on the 6th of December, or at least to protect me in some way or anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you convey this to General Kadijevic at the time, how you were feeling?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you've just said, did you view yourself as what we refer to as a scapegoat?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not how I viewed myself. But all the circumstances led to me turning out to be the main perpetrator, and I had taken every measure in order to stop this from happening, as if someone was pulling all the threads so that all of this would happen to me. And I never dreamt of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you explain to General Kadijevic that whatever measures you had tried to take as to this incident or previous incidents involving shelling of the Old Town had not met with support of General Strugar? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you return to Podgorica or when did you leave Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think sometime around 1630 hours, around 1700 hours, I believe. I don't know exactly. I had proposed some measures to General Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, you have just a moment ago mentioned that, "I had taken every measure in order to stop this from happening, as if someone was pulling all the threads so that all of this would happen to me." Who did you mean by "someone"? Did you have anybody in mind when you said, "Someone was pulling the threads"?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. At that time, of course, I didn't know anything about it. It was only later that I investigated this. And during all these 13 years, I tried to establish the truth, how this attack came about. And I think that the truth is out now, except for some minor details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after -- at this point in time, looking at it now, do you have any view of who that someone who was pulling the threads may have been?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot point a finger, and I cannot say that it was General Strugar who ordered that. That would not be right. That would not correspond to the facts, or rather I cannot prove that. But I do believe that many or some people who were close to him were giving support, or rather encouraging the attack on the 6th of December. General Strugar -- General Strugar supported the story of Kovacevic, and he was saying that he was not responsible or guilty on account of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That who was not responsible or guilty?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that General Strugar supported the story of Captain Kovacevic, that he did not intentionally attack Srdj, that he did not intentionally shell Dubrovnik and so on. He supported that story, and he protected him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what I'm asking you, though, is you said that: "He was not responsible or guilty on account of that." Who are you referring to when you say, "He is not responsible."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I meant Captain Kovacevic because I investigated --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you of a different opinion?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you suggesting, from the vantage point today, that persons under the command and control of General Strugar are the persons you're referring to as having supported the activities on the 6th of December, the attack and all that followed on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the return from Podgorica, did you discuss with General Strugar the measures to be taken in relation to the shelling?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. From Podgorica, we went to Trebinje, to his command post. And then from Trebinje to Kupari, to my command post. As we travelled, we talked, especially at his command post in Trebinje, about the further steps that were to be taken. It was accepted that the official version of the events of the 6th of December, which was composed at the command of the 2nd Operational Group on the basis of information provided by Captain Kovacevic, which was given by his officers, that this official version of the event should be sent to Belgrade to the General Staff, and that I should stand by that story, that version, at the press conference on the following day. And that press conference was held in Kupari. Likewise, I suggested, and General Strugar agreed, that on the following day, I sign the peace agreement, initial the peace agreement, or rather the cease-fire, and that I send my team of officers to Dubrovnik to assess the damage in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who accepted? It was accepted. What did you mean by "accepted"? Who accepted it? Who gave the instructions to adopt a certain version of the facts?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Strugar instructed me as to what we should accept, what we should do. It was this official version of the events that took place on the 6th of December. That is to say, that I should stand by that at the press conference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you suggest the removal of Captain Kovacevic to General Strugar on the way back?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I tried to say that a while ago. During the meeting with General Kadijevic, towards the end of my remarks, I offered my resignation, and I proposed that Captain Kovacevic be removed from the position of the commander of the 3rd Battalion and that an investigation be carried out and that he be sent to Court. Those were my proposals and requests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Strugar agree with the removal of General Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. General Strugar did not say anything at the meeting. But after that, he did not agree with it. I'm sorry. I forgot. I proposed that the 3rd Battalion be taken out of the combat deployment because of their lack of reliability. However, he did not agree with that. Also, he did not agree with the removal of Captain Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the version of the facts that you indicated you were instructed by General Strugar to adopt prove to be false? Or was it apparent at the time that it was false?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, everything was not clear. It wasn't clear to me for sure, but I believe that everything was not clear to him either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you propose to issue an apology or an expression of regret to the Croatian side and to the intermediary European monitors for the events, for the shelling of the 6th?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I suggested to him, but he did not accept that. Not only then, but also before that when they informed me around 9.00 from the Crisis Staff in Dubrovnik, that's when I expressed my regrets, when I established that it was actually true that shells were falling on the town. I expressed my regrets then, and I said that I had not ordered that, that this was an arbitrary attack by a lower-ranking commander and that he would be taken to task and held responsible. I ordered fire to stop. And then I sent a telex to Minister Rudolf. In this telex, I repeated this yet again stating that General Kadijevic had also ordered an investigation. Although I was not quite sure of that, but I did write it nevertheless. However, General Strugar said to me that we would not apologise to anyone, and that extremists from Srdj were to be blamed, volunteers. Something was said along that lines -- along those lines, because of the losses that Captain Kovacevic had sustained on account of that and that that is why he set out to take revenge for those killed soldiers. I absolutely accepted this first part, and that is what I said to the journalists, that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which first part is that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first part, that the commander of the battalion was provoked by the attack from the Croatian side, that he had one casualty, that is to say, one man dead and two men wounded, and that is why he launched an attack, in order to avenge his soldiers. I said that to journalists, that that sometimes happens during war, that a commander loses it and then he wants to take revenge. However, I said further on that this was an arbitrary attack and that this battalion commander would be held accountable, that an investigation would be ordered and that it would be carried out. I said that because I believed that that is what would really happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew at the time, did you not, that this was not the case, that this was false and that you could not justify any type of shelling with retaliation or reprisal? That is not acceptable --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I asked you about apologies, you said "I told him." To whom where you -- when you said "him" and that he did not agree, to whom were you referring?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your assessment as to which units shelled the Old Town on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until I came from Belgrade, I thought that it was only the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade took part in the shelling. However, when Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I came to my command post in Kupari, they notified me that in addition to the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade, this attack upon the request of Captain Kovacevic was supported twice by the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade which was across Rijeka Dubrovacka. And --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you proceed, my question to you was about the Old Town. Which formations, which units shelled the Old Town? You have answered me that other units were involved in the attack generally, but which units shelled the Old Town as far as you determined?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the shelling of the Old Town, only the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade could have done it, and they were the only ones who did operate against the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of that formation, that unit?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Captain Vladimir Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the same battalion that was introduced in November, and after its introduction to the combat theatre, the Old Town was shelled?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just add one thing: However, at that time, it was not on its own in front of Dubrovnik. At that time, we were not sure because there were other battalions of the brigade there, and at that time, in November, it was the entire brigade artillery that could have targeted the Old Town. So we were not sure that it was only that battalion that did it, although there was suspicion even then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the fact that it was one of the battalions that could have or that was -- yes, that could have been involved in the November shellings, is there a relationship to your conclusion also about its involvement in the December shelling? Did you factor that into it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, of course. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were telling us about the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade. Can you please continue. Just indicate what you learned about the involvement of that battalion during the attack and how it came to be involved. Did you yourself know at the time it was involved?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time, I did not know it. When I returned from Belgrade, I heard about how this had happened. When Captain Kovacevic took Srdj, and when he started suffering lethal artillery fire from the town of Dubrovnik, and since he did not have the artillery support from my units because Captain Kozaric sent him a message that he would never be supported by sector artillery, he then asked his colleague, the commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade who was behind Rijeka Dubrovacka to target with his artillery those points that he could not reach outside the Old Town. That was Lapad, Babin Kuk, where there were cannons belonging to the Croatian Defence, cannons that were of larger calibre. From there, he was targeting his soldiers at Srdj, and he did sustain losses. This colleague of his, Lieutenant Colonel Jovanovic, engaged in fire twice with his mortars of 120 and 82 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will ask you in a minute about the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will ask you in a minute about the weaponry of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade. But I have a question based on something you said. Considering that the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade was one of the battalions that you viewed as having potential culpability in the November shellings against the Old Town, and considering that you had wanted the entire brigade removed, is it your view that if the 3rd Battalion had been removed, the shelling that occur on the 6th of December may not have occurred? Do you see a relationship between the two events?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely, I do see a relationship, because had there been a mixed unit of the Territorial Defence that was still there or a battalion of the Territorial Defence of Trebinje or any other unit, these events of the 6th of December would not have happened. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your view, leaving in place heavy weaponry with units who had shown willingness to use such weaponry against areas prohibited from being shelled, do you see a link between that and the - I'm referring to November - do you see a link between that and the events of the 6th of December, the shelling of the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you continue to hold the view that troops should be thinned out and that weaponry should be withdrawn? And if you did, do you see a link to the failure to implement that to the events of the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now that this event already happened, now the mosaic has fallen into place, and now everything is quite clear. It was hard for me to make an additional request to pull out the 3rd Battalion or, rather, for it not to remain in those positions at all, because I did not have clear grounds. There had not been an investigation in November that had established that Captain Kovacevic and his battalion were the sole perpetrators. So all of this had to do with suspicions only, reasonable doubt certainly, but we didn't have more than that in terms of him being the sole perpetrator. However, if that unit had not been there, the Old Town would not have been shelled on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, your conclusion as to the unit which shelled the Old Town, you've identified as the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade, can you please give us some of the bases for your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One did not have to investigate in order to establish that it was only that unit with regard to the position of their arms that could shell the city on that day, on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your notification about the shelling of the Old Town, as you indicated earlier, came through Mr. Rudolf, Minister Rudolf?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you conduct an investigation into the shelling?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I tried to carry out investigation upon my return from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do? Explain how you carried out the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to the command post in Kupari, I asked all the participants, the battalion commander, the Chief of Staff, my deputy Zec and Colonel Kovacevic and Kozaric, the captain, I asked them to give me their written reports, and I investigated as much as possible what had happened on that same evening. I was told then they issued their reports. I listened to them. And then I was told that Captain Kovacevic was in such a state of shock that he was beyond control because of the losses that he had suffered in his units, and that he was not able to issue any statements or reports and that he was not able to come and see me in Kupari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were not able to have any interview with Captain Kovacevic, neither you nor any of your officers who may have been designated to speak with the parties involved?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I sent my officers to his battalion. My four officers went there to talk to others, to establish what had happened, and to help this unit to reinforce their state of morale after all the losses that they had suffered. I asked them to spend the entire night with that unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you, Admiral. What type of losses? Numbers?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 5 dead and 14 wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over the course of the Dubrovnik combat, did you have any observation about the numbers of losses that Captain Kovacevic's battalion suffered relative to the overall losses for the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that this battalion had more losses than the entire brigade up to that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these losses incurred -- who was commanding the battalion when these losses were incurred?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to the 25th of October, the commander was Ekrem Devlic, Major Devlic, and he was seriously injured on the 24th of October. And then Captain Kovacevic took over. Up to then, he was deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at all times Captain Kovacevic was in one way or the other either commander or deputy commander of this battalion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the losses that were incurred, do you know how they were incurred? Where they were incurred? Was it perhaps in response or from responsive fire from Croat positions? Did you have any information?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know exactly about all the circumstances before the brigade came under my command. However, very often I would receive information that losses were incurred by wrong command, lack of discipline, fire, a lack of reconnaissance, failure to take shelter, provocation on both sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 6th, the losses on the 6th of December, did you come to learn how they were incurred?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were incurred in battles for the mount -- for Mount Srdj. When Mount Srdj was taken, then the entire artillery from the city of Dubrovnik opened fire on that unit. The terrain was not covered, and that's how losses were incurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you ask you to clarify something. You have in the past referred to the town of Dubrovnik and the city. When you use the term "town" or "city" without the term "Old Town," are you referring to the overall municipal Dubrovnik area? Just so we can distinguish. Excluding the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about the artillery outside the old city walls. I'm talking about the fire positions of the artillery that belonged to the defence of the town of Dubrovnik, which was outside of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The reason I ask you is earlier on, much earlier in your testimony, you talked about warning sent to the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff that civilians and citizens of Dubrovnik should be removed from the weapons of, and you said, "The town," that were being used to fire in order to reduce civilian casualties. Was that reference to the city, the main part of the city outside the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. It was on the 10th of November that the call came from the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Admiral. What did you find out from the statements of the individuals that were taken by the officers you assigned to interview them? What had the company commanders of the 3rd Battalion and those at Zarkovica informed your officers? I'm going to ask you to try to move at a relatively rapid pace given the time considerations.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, there were not that many details with regard to the conversations with company commanders. They were not willing to talk because of the losses, because of the casualties. They were very sad. So they didn't offer too much information to my officers. The only thing that was clear was that fire had been opened from Srdj on Captain Kovacevic's unit, and according to that information he had one dead and two injured soldiers up to 6.00 in the morning of the 6th of December. Based on that, he decided that one part of the battalion, the 3rd Company, would start moving towards Srdj and that the 1st Company from Bosanka forward, that he would also start moving towards Mount Srdj in order to prevent provocations and take the facility on Mount Srdj. When he took it, around 10.00 in the morning, fierce fire was opened from town. More losses were incurred. And that's when the drama started with regard to the withdrawal of his units and shelling of the Old Town and some parts of the area outside the Old Town walls. However, their statements, according to which the artillery of the 3rd Battalion opened fire on the weapons that had inflicted losses upon them in the vicinity of the Old Town, in the vicinity of the towers of the Old Town where they had discovered mortars. And according to them, they did not shell the Old Town directly. The only thing that they wanted to do was neutralise those mortars that were incurring their losses. And that's the essence of what they had learned from them. The same story repeated that was offered in November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they tell you the losses that were incurred? What was their version?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their version was as follows: Cannons and mortars from the town outside the Old Town or in the vicinity of the towers of the Old Town opened fire on them in an encovered [as interpreted] area and incurred their losses. And there was also suspicion that there were arms in the Old Town itself. This, however, was never confirmed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand it, this is their version, the version given by the officers involved in the attack on that day, on the 6th. Did you necessarily accept this version as having truth, or as the true version of the facts?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had my doubts about that from the very beginning, and I expressed my suspicion. And I said to the Chief of Staff that I couldn't believe that he could not stop the attack together with Colonel Kovacevic and prevent the shelling while it lasted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you come to learn -- or did you ever come to find that fire was, in fact, not initiated from Srdj, but rather initiated by the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Subsequently I established that. And especially during the period when I managed to get hold of company commanders and battalion commanders. And then I spoke with Captain Kovacevic when he was free, and I managed to talk to him openly about certain things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was before my departure to The Hague. He told me that Captain Zec had told him when he arrived at Mount Zarkovica that the Admiral was very angry, that he would not get artillery support, that he should finish off what he had started and withdraw. These were his words. And I quote him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "This is before my departure to The Hague. He told me that Captain Zec told him," who is "he"?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did this take place, this conversation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Belgrade, just before my departure for The Hague. I had a meeting with him. I wanted to learn the truth, regardless of how serious it may have been for any of the parties involved. And it was then that I finally concluded that both of them, Colonel Kovacevic and Captain Zec, sabotaged my decision and my request to cease fire immediately. I had my doubts about that, even before, but it was then that I reached my final conclusion to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you factor into your conclusion about believing or not believing Captain Kovacevic's version the type of weapons that were at the disposal of the Croatian forces at Srdj? I say that as the indication or the allegation that there was lethal fire coming from Srdj and that an artillery attack by the 3rd Battalion had to be undertaken. What was your view of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Somers. I haven't understood there was lethal fire from defenders from Srdj. I understood it was from parts of Dubrovnik, but not the Old Town --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The city, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- directed at Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The type of fire that was coming from Srdj, what could that have been?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to Srdj or to the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was infantry fire from automatic rifles, and they also had two machine-guns on Mount Srdj. But they didn't have artillery. And it could not have been lethal for the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of response, if there were any truth to the allegation that the Croatian forces attacked that morning, what type of response would a reasonable commander or would a commander of a battalion have taken to that type of fire?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that fire had been lethal, as they claimed, from the front part of the defence, from Srdj and Nuncijata and the Belvedere Hotel, a reasonable commander should have responded with adequate fire which he had at his disposal and neutralise that fire. So he had to prevent that infantry fire, and he had at his disposal everything in order to do that. He should not have used artillery and mortars. Because the attack was still not fully fledged up to the point when the town had to be shelled. Only the front lines of the Croatian Defence from which provocation fire started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated that you believe that Captain Zec and Colonel Kovacevic had sabotaged the operation or the mission you had sent them to do. What -- can you explain that, please. Did you sense these officers individually, or was there some collusive action you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that this was a concert activity, that this was organised. However, from 8.00 in the morning when Captain Zec arrived in Zarkovica and immediately upon that Colonel Kovacevic followed, up to 12.00, so for the period of four hours, they could talk Captain Kovacevic into abandoning the position. And they could prevent further artillery attack on the town, if they had been determined to do so, and if they acted -- had acted professionally, and if they had executed my express order for the unit to be stopped and returned to their initial positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, did you undertake any discipline toward Captain Kovacevic for submitting what you believed to be a false report?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't manage to go -- to get hold of Captain Kovacevic at all. At my request for him to finally come and see me, I was told that he had previous commitments, that he had to attend funerals of his dead soldiers, and those funerals were taking place all over Montenegro. Once this was done, then General Panic visited, and this is the first time I saw him after the incidents that took place on the 6th of December. But it seems to me that he was given advice to leave the unit for a while. However, I can't prove that. Everybody knew that I wanted to remove him from this position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, in his report, did Captain Kovacevic allege or assert that his positions had come under fire from the Old Town and was this probable?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In his official report which he actually didn't write himself as far as I understand, I don't know who participated in the writing of this report, he claimed that fire had been opened on his unit from the front part, from Srdj and Nuncijata and Belvedere Hotel, as well as from the town itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the town, are you referring to the parts outside of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is not referring to the Old Town; he's referring to the town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you forward to General Strugar the report of Captain Kovacevic? And if you did, what was General Strugar's reaction or attitude towards it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His attitude was that this report reflected the truth, that it was credible, and he believed in that all this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your investigations, you mentioned that you learned that the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade had become involved. Who was the commander of that battalion and was it under your command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander was Major Srboljub Zdravkovic. He was absent from his unit at the time. His deputy was Lieutenant Miroslav Jovanovic. He had been sent by his unit in Podgorica to replace the commander of the battalion during his absence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how can you explain getting support from another -- from one battalion to another? Did it go through you? Did it go through your operations officer? How could this happen? Are you necessary in that particular activity?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. That was a battalion under my command. And without my express order, they were not supposed to open fire or participate in operations. Until my return from Belgrade, I didn't know that they had opened fire because they only opened fire on two occasions for ten minutes. Its positions were far from Kupari, and we did not hear fire being opened from their artillery. The distance between their positions and the command post was about 25 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then explain if you had to be -- if you had to give your authorisation, how did they communicate? How did they get the support? How did Captain Kovacevic get support from Jovanovic? Support fire.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I did not explain that. It all starts with the units. Their initial positions are able to communicate between themselves.
