The 3rd Battalion of the 472nd can communicate with the 5th Brigade independently of me. They can communicate through the communications centre without my knowledge. And when they started suffering losses, Captain Kovacevic did not receive my artillery support. He phoned his colleague and asked him to neutralise the artillery fire in the Babin Kuk, Lapad, Petka sector, and some hotels were -- mortar positions were outside of the Old Town. This battalion could not reach as far as the Old Town from their position. The 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the use of naval units in the course of the day in connection with the attack on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The naval units, that is, ships, did not open fire on the 6th of December. This was not planned. We didn't know that it would occur. The ships did not have any orders. And this can be confirmed by the commander of the defence of the town of Dubrovnik. He can confirm that the ships did not open fire on that day or around that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on all of the information that you have assessed, how would you characterise the shelling of the Old Town of Dubrovnik on the 6th of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in no other way but this being a wilful attack, illegal, in contravention of all explicit orders of Superior Commands. And it was only the commander of the 3rd Battalion who could have been responsible for it because he was the one who had issued the order to shell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any views on other factors that -- or what factors may have supported your conclusion that it was a deliberate attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection. This word "deliberate" cannot be found in the previous answer. I cannot see it. And I did not hear that word being used in B/C/S. I did not hear the Admiral use it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'll be happy to substitute that word for "wilful." I see them as synonymous, but I will be happy to use the word wilful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, let me rephrase my question. Do you have any views on other factors that have supported your conclusion that it was a wilful attack?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- well, first of all, when we are talking about a wilful attack, I mean the way the attack started against Srdj. That's how the attack started. This attack later on developed further due to the losses sustained when the attack was launched further on the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, I want to make sure we're understanding each other. When you say "wilful," what do you mean by wilful? And I'm talking only about the shelling of the Old Town of Dubrovnik on the 6th of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wish to say is the following: That the attack was wilful. But at first, it was not aimed against the Old Town. That's not what I meant. I think that it was aimed at Srdj only. And in order to take Srdj and destroy all of those who were at Srdj. That was the idea of those who were planning this, protecting it, supporting it. But the idea was not to attack the Old Town. That is what I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the Old Town was attacked, how do you come to the conclusion that it was wilful once it was attacked? And it may help, Admiral, if I say attack --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Your Honour, I think we have a problem which has been appearing for a few days now due to the interpretation. In the B/C/S language, the witness has been saying "samovoljan," in the sense of not having been ordered, that is to say, an arbitrary decision of someone who launched an attack. I have the impression, though, that this description is being interpreted as "wilful." I'm not sure that the word "wilful" in the English language corresponds to what the witness means when he says "samovoljan," what he means when testifying before this Trial Chamber. I believe that there was confusion on that account, a very meaningful one, because these are two completely different things, or rather in the Serbian version of the B/C/S language. So I think that this should be clarified in detail because the witness keeps talking about "samovoljan."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Arbitrariness, wilfulness says the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But it turns out to be different. So what the interpretation of "samovoljan" should be self-initiative, or at his own initiative. That is what it should say, not "wilful." Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, if you could explore that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, you have heard the discussion about linguistic differences, and so that we are clear, I want to ask you what factors -- first of all, if by the term "wilful" in your language you are referring to the -- let me ask you, what aspect are you referring to when you use the term "wilful"? Can you explain that, and then perhaps we can explore that a little further.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wish to say by that is that the decision concerning the attack was made by Captain Kovacevic, without receiving orders from his Superior Command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Considering the duration of the shelling of the Old Town, the intensity of the shelling of the Old Town, the weapons used during the shelling of the Old Town, what is your view -- how would you characterise the shelling of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's hard for me to say that from the very first moment the idea of the battalion commander was to attack the Old Town straight away. It is hard for me to say that. And I cannot claim that. However, as soon as he started suffering losses, it is hard for me to say at what time, what the hour was. But I think that already as of 8.00 in the morning, shells started falling on the Old Town because I heard about that during the telephone conversation I had with Minister Rudolf. Now, whether he intended to attack the Old Town immediately in the morning is something that I cannot believe at all, but the shelling of the Old Town did start at 8.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given the weaponry that was used or that was available to the battalion, is it your view that Captain Kovacevic knew he was shelling the Old Town, he or units under his command and control were shelling Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that absolutely, from the position where he commanded from and from the observation post, that he had to know that and see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Zarkovica, would you -- is there an obstructed or unobstructed view of the Old Town of Dubrovnik from Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unobstructed. Everything can be seen clearly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you question the three senior officers you sent to Zarkovica regarding the incident? The senior officers Zec, Colonel Kovacevic, and I think it's Djurasic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the results of your inquiry of these three persons?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that the result was that he was responding to the gunfire coming from Srdj and from the front end where he had incurred losses from, and that therefore he was out to destroy the defenders at Srdj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. You said: As I said that the result was that he was responding to, could you please clarify? Did you mean to say, "I said" or, "He said"? My question was: And what were the results of your inquiry to these three persons? And the transcript shows is, "Well, I said that the result was that..." Who was speaking? Who said?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These officers of mine said that they had found out that Captain Kovacevic had started the attack because he was provoked by gunfire coming from the front end of the Croatian Defence and because of the losses that he had suffered. And that that is why he started this wilful attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you view that your senior officers then as well were giving false reports?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, of course, I had suspicions regarding that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a commission of investigation that you ordered to be put into action to conduct an assessment of damage to the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As for the damage, yes, I did propose this, and General Strugar accepted it, and Minister Rudolf did, too, that a team of officers should be sent from my command who would tour the Old Town and assess the extent of the damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did this happen? And who were the officers, please?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was done on the 8th after the agreement had been initialled. On the 8th of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 8th of what?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 8th of December, a three-member commission from my command toured the Old Town and compiled a report about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was the 8th of December 1991, some two days after the incident?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the officers whom you sent? The names, please, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't recall this very instant. But the names are on the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there a means of recording the damage that these officers saw?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They mentioned point by point the damage that they had established for themselves and seen for themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they memorialise it? Was there some form of memorialisation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they made a report. I'm sorry. I forgot to mention something. They also recorded two diskettes about this damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Audio or video?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Videocassettes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the videocassettes? Did you see whatever they --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you have rated or how would you have characterised the damage resulting from the 6th of December that you observed in the videofootage? Would you have characterised it -- well, how would you have characterised it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I saw, and which was presented on these diskettes, were not terrible damages. It wasn't total destruction. I characterised it as damage. I don't know whether I gave any particular qualification as to the level or degree of that damage. But I don't think that it was major damage. I don't think that it was destructive. I think that's the word I used, and perhaps that's the word I could use now, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the word that you used at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you presented with a finding of the commission, a report which you had to author -- to sign off on?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was -- at the time, was there a complete, transparent, thorough investigation conducted as to the damage in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Perhaps I should explain this better. In that report of mine, I did not qualify the damage as far as I can remember. I just signed the report. And I said the following: That these were the findings of the commission --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I was just going to ask if everyone would turn to tab 32 of their binders, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, Admiral?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the document, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... that came out of your command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the document dated the 9th of December and sent to Admiral Stane Brovet, deputy Federal Secretariat for National Defence, with my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this investigation carried out in connection with orders by General Kadijevic to investigate?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is Admiral Brovet?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was General Kadijevic's deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was General Strugar aware of the fact that there was an investigation ordered by General Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Kadijevic did not order an investigation of the entire incident of the shelling of the Old Town on the 6th of December. I just said to you that I had proposed to have an investigation and to have Captain Kovacevic removed and so on. However, towards the end of what I was saying, and when I also offered my resignation, General Kadijevic said something to the effect of, "Go down there, repair the damage, let there be no greater consequences, finish this successfully," and so on and so forth, along those lines. He did not explicitly order to carry out an investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was General Strugar present at this conversation you just talked about?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at this document, Admiral, it is, "Conclusions of a commission." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And identifies a commission of 9th Naval District Boka compromising of Major Boskovic, Colonel Pesic, and a Savo Jovanovic, a cameraman, visiting old parts of Dubrovnik on the 8th of December, 1991, between 1000 and 1400 hours. This is the group that you were referring to before whose names you were not necessarily able to recall?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are these are the people you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, your answer?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. A quick question. How did these individuals from the JNA, from your formation which is part of the 2nd Operational Group of the JNA, how did they manage to get into Dubrovnik? What was their means of being allowed into the city? What were the logistics of this, if you can very briefly describe it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the 7th of December, when I initialled the agreement, I agreed with Minister Rudolf that he should let the team members in because they were to investigate the damage. So they entered Dubrovnik as there was a cease-fire in place, so they had free passage. And they were met there. And together with the members of the Crisis Staff, they toured all the places where the destruction had actually occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And above the -- sorry. A very quick run through, literally just a moment on each point: "First point, visible traces of damage on some houses caused by small-calibre shells. Damage is minor and can be repaired in a short time. Signs of damage were noticed on the following facilities and were recorded. One, Church of St. Blaise, slightly damaged in two places on the facade from shell ricochet and one metre of the fence. Two, the Stradun pedestrian promenade, street damaged in 15 places in the form of superficial holes with a radius of 35 to 50 centimetres. Three, a house of Rudjer Boskovic, the parapet demolished and one lintel slightly damaged. Four, opposite house on Siroka Street, one corner at the top of the building slightly damaged. Five, five buildings burned down, the cause of the fire could not be determined on the spot. Six, the Onofrio fountain, one hit to the dome."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, there are 20 items listed. Do you need to read all of them?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I wanted to give a sampling of the description. I have no intention of going through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, when you saw that these items as described were in a protected area, did you ask for any further clarification, any further investigation of the damage that's reported? Or did you just accept what the commission gave you at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accepted the findings of the commission because that is what Admiral Brovet had asked for first and foremost. So I just signed this and sent it. I did not give any qualifications. I did not present any opinions of my own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the very end: "It is the opinion of the commission that there is no substantial damage to the cultural and historical monuments. The origin of all the damage cannot be stated with certainty or the perpetrators named because it is obvious that a lot of the damage was not caused by attacks from outside of the Old Town centre." Now, Admiral, was this part of the climate of denial that appears to have been permeating through all the discussions about culpability as to the attack on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think you're right, yes. If you wish, I can explain on this specific example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have another question, though. The damage that is listed here and the damage that was seen, would you really -- do you concur that it is minor? Did you come to learn later about a different state of description of damage?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, it was considered that this was not major damage, that it was damage of smaller proportions. It was even being said that some of the damage was done intentionally, meaning the torching of wooden houses or houses that had wooden roofs, not to go into all of that now. However, later on, of course, it was established that the damages were of greater proportions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You began to explain my question about the climate of denial. Would you please continue with what you were going to say.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I meant to say: This denial or shifting the guilt to the other side, it did exist then. And I think that this was another example of hushing things up or hushing the guilt of JNA units up. My opinion was then, and today I think, that evident facts cannot be hushed up and that professionalism of the units of the Yugoslav People's Army cannot be proven by shifting the blame to the other side. Had an investigation been ordered and carried out then, a true investigation regarding the shelling of Dubrovnik, I think that the JNA would have gained far more in terms of its reputation and dignity, rather than that mountain of orders stating that we should not target the Old Town, that we should be disciplined, that all sorts of measures should be taken. And in practice, these orders were not observed. I think that that is the truth of the matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Not observed" by whom, Admiral? These orders were not observed by whom?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically in this case, the commander of the 3rd Battalion. But also certain officers who gave support or protection to such an arbitrary and grave offence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this non-observance tolerated by all levels of command above?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask at this point, please, to move into evidence the 9th -- I'm sorry, I'm informed that it has a number. It does. P61 for reference for the Registrar. Apparently, it's a previous... And it's tab 39 of P61. It must have been a composite exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the reason in your view that a thorough, complete investigation was not conducted by you? Why did you not complete a thorough investigation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this unit, the 3rd Battalion, was temporarily resubordinated to me. It was not within my establishment. It was within the establishment of the 472nd Brigade, which was subordinated to the 2nd Operational Group. So for an investigation that I would carry out with my authorities, I would have to receive orders from the commander of the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did such orders come through? Did you receive such orders for an investigation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. A thorough and real investigation regarding this case was not wanted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think everybody from the General Staff -- let me start from there, and the commander of the operational group, and at my level, my level, including me. But I personally wanted even then, and I did do what I was in a position to do. However, when General Panic came and when orders were issued that there should be decorations and commendations for persons participating in this event, that was something that came as total discouragement to me. And officially, I could not do anything any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please indicate, who is General Panic? When did he come and where did he come to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, he was deputy chief of General Staff. And he came to the command of the 2nd Operational Group. And near Dubrovnik --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was on the 12th of December. The 12th or the 14th of December. So he came to establish, as far as I know, what had happened on the 6th of December and to see this for himself. And then he observed from Zarkovica both the Old Town and listened to the explanations of the commander of the 3rd Battalion and some of his company commanders in the presence of General Strugar and in my presence, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Strugar make any particular request of Captain Kovacevic in the presence of General Panic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end, when he finished, he asked Captain Kovacevic to propose two commanders for decoration, the ones that were the most prominent during the events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the events of what? During what events?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the 12th or the 14th of December, and the events were combat operations in which those commanders played a prominent role. So we're talking about the month of November and the events on the 6th of December in which this certain battalion participated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to make sure I understand because it is not entirely clear to me. Who recommended that the names be presented for commendation for these combat operations? Who recommended to General Panic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to General Panic. I didn't say General Panic. I said General Strugar had ordered Captain Kovacevic to propose the names of two of his company commanders who played the most prominent role in the combat operations that took place on the 6th of December and between the 10th to 12th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was done in the presence of General Panic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Captain Kovacevic do that? Did he obey the order of General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you there? Did you witness this yourself?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, did you attempt to have any further investigation, inquiry, or discipline inquiry concerning the events of the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, were you aware of any steps that were taken within the command of the 2nd Operational Group to investigate the incident or to take any measures against those responsible for the shelling on the 6th of December, the shelling of the Old Town on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any promotion that Captain Kovacevic may have gotten during that period? Actually, if we can turn to tab 41, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is an exhibit with a number of pages. And perhaps if the hard copy could be given to Admiral Jokic, it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, you have before you a document which is a personnel file, part of a personnel file of Captain First Class Vladimir Kovacevic. Are you familiar with this type of document, Admiral?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not seen this before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with personnel files, Admiral, this type of dossier? Is this something that you have -- generally?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this appear to be a personnel file with Captain Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you turn to the page that has at the top of it the numbers 03390469. That is in B/C/S. And let me see if I can find the...

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And in English, Your Honours, it would be, on the translation, page -- looks like it's page 1 of the translation, where it says, "For permission, promotion."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you find there any promotions that occurred in the year 1991? If you find such a promotion, can you read across and indicate what is said about the promotion.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here, what is described is an extraordinary promotion in to captain first class. This was ordered by the Federal Secretariat for National Defence on the 14th December 1991. And the number of this order is 7-173. The extraordinary promotion was carried out on the 11th of November 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean it was retroactive? It went back to the time of 11 November 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was an extraordinary promotion, and it was retroactive, referring back to the 11th November 1991. All the regular promotions in the JNA took place on the 22nd of December. This, however, was an extraordinary promotion, and the order was issued on the 14 December. And it was retroactive as of the 11 November 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see any other promotions for Captain Kovacevic listed on that page? And if so, the date, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 11th November 1995 -- I apologise. On the 21st of February, 1996, Captain Kovacevic was promoted to the rank of major. Again, retroactively as of 11 November 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you move along a bit, do you see any document that indicates when Captain Kovacevic separated from his military service? If you look at the top of 03390501 in Serbo-Croatian, the document that bears the signature of Commander Colonel Miroslav Filipovic. Do you see that document, Admiral?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. Again, this is a decision issued by Colonel Miroslav Filipovic on the termination of service for Captain Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the date for termination of service?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 5th of April 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just briefly, who was Miroslav Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miroslav Filipovic was the -- Major Kovacevic's commander in VP2322, Pozarevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a part of the 2nd Operational Group during October, November, and December of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was the chief of the operational department in the command of the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to what you've described as an extraordinary promotion in 1991, from December 14th, 1991 retroactive to November, on whose recommendation would a subordinate officer be given a promotion?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the recommendation of his command, of his unit, I assume, the unit that was superior to the 3rd Battalion, which means that his brigade was his Superior Command, the 472nd Brigade. And it was only this brigade that could issue such proposal, such recommendation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recommend this promotion, or did you have any support for his promotion?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that everybody was astonished about this extraordinary promotion, the person who had to be taken to task and who had to stand trial for what he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can a promotion like this go through if the command of the 2nd Operational Group does not agree with it or does not recommend it or does not veto it? Either approve, recommend, or veto?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure is as follows: All the subordinated commands, subordinated to the 2nd Operational Group deliver their proposals for extraordinary promotions. This is then gathered in the operational group. It is approved or not, and the approvals are then referred to the General Staff. That is the procedure. And if the 2nd Operational Group rejects the proposal, it would not be forwarded to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask to move this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Document P133.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just in summary, then, Admiral, based on what you just explained, what is your understanding of General Strugar's approval or disapproval of the promotion of Captain Kovacevic? Talking about the one in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He approved it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can ask, please, to take a quick look at tab 33. Admiral, before I ask you to look at the document in front of you, I want to ask you something -- one more point about the promotion, and we're talking about Captain Kovacevic still. If he receives a promotion with effect to -- retroactive effect to 11th of November, what is that for? What type of activity is that type of promotion for, given what is happening -- given what the units are doing?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were talking in great detail about the period between the 10th and 12th of November when this battalion took Strincjera and Gradac for us and the entire area of Dubrovnik in front of Srdj. So this promotion would refer to the successful activities of that battalion and the taking of Vitares in front of Mount Srdj during the Dubrovnik campaign which took place in November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are those the same combat operations during the course of which the Old Town of Dubrovnik was shelled?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Taking a look at what is admittedly only two pages of a larger bulletin, I wanted to ask you simply about language. This is a bulletin that is for -- it is a bulletin. Do you recognise this type of publication? Are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the information service of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence which carries information about various events. In this particular case, we're talking about promotions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in this particular case, we're looking at communication of the service. It's called FSND Information Service, Belgrade, November 29th, by decree of the Yugoslav Presidency of November 28, 1991, the following officers have been promoted to higher ranks for successful directing and commanding exceptional conduct in action and carrying out combat assignments of a particular importance for the armed forces in the defence of country. And then it lists some names. To the rank of Colonel General, Lieutenant Generals Panic, Pavle A. Strugar, and Nikola M. Uzelac. Are you familiar with the promotions that are referred to in this particular bulletin?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I ask to move this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is P134.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the reference to 28 November, that is eight days before the shelling of the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And language indicates: "Successful directing and commanding." They are talking about General Strugar's promotion for successful directing and commanding?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask you to look at tab 42, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just before we leave that tab, I wonder whether the Admiral can clarify the rank to which this promotion was. Can you tell us, Admiral, whether this is a rank of three-star or how many stars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this rank is of a general, three-star.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, in front of you is a document which is personnel file. Again, you have indicated that you're familiar with personnel files. And you've shown that some of the entries there include promotion. This is a file for General Pavle Strugar. I would ask you to take a look in the Serbo-Croatian version on page that has at the top 03390543. Do you see a section that deals with promotions on that page?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the page, is there an indication of a promotion for General Strugar? If so, to what rank, what type of promotion, and what date?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Lieutenant Colonel by degree of the Presidency of the SFRY. The number is 1/64. The date is 28 November. Extraordinary promotion effective as of 26 November 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just moving very quickly to the page that has 03390668 in your language, a document signed by General -- Lieutenant Colonel General Momcilo Perisic, does that document indicate the date of General Strugar's separation from military service?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This decision was issued on the 31st of December, 1993. And by this decision, General Strugar was separated from his active military service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his rank at the time of separation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel General.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask to move this into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is P135.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, in your view, what are the underlying reasons for the 6th of December shelling of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be absolutely sure about the motives because those motives were neither rational or reasonable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking motives. What do you view, based on what you have told us today, what do you view, not just today but over the course of your testimony, as the underlying reasons for the shelling of the 6th of December of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to give you all the reasons, the reasons that were put forth and were not correct and those that were actually correct. One of the reasons that was given to me in this half-investigation was that cannons around the Old Town were shelled in order to neutralise them. And that's why shells started falling on the Old Town. I'm now going to give you the true reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you for justifications. I'm asking you for underlying reasons that have to do with what was going on in your command area. I'm not asking for justifications for the various excuses. The reasons that the shelling of the Old Town of Dubrovnik on the 6th of December could occur given the history of everything that you have told us.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, one of the reasons was to shell the weapons around the Old Town. The second one was to inflict damage on the Old Town. Another one was to retaliate for the dead and wounded in the 3rd Battalion. Also, to punish the command -- the former commander of the 472nd Brigade who had fled to Dubrovnik. And they considered this to be one part of the retaliation as well. So there were multiple reasons. But the main reason was to inflict damage on the town, on the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you find a connection, a link, between the enforcement of orders toward the Old Town prior to the 6th of December, the enforcement or non-enforcement, and the events of the shelling of the Old Town on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. There is a link. In November, there was an investigation -- if there had been an investigation and if the culprit had been identified, there wouldn't have been the shelling on the 6th of December. And I can agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm going to try to skip through things really quickly. I just need a second to review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I think we might skip through them after the break, Ms. Somers. We'll have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, having indicated just before the break that there was a link between the lack of investigation in November and the failure to take measures for the shellings against the Old Town in November and the events of the 6th of December, can you explain why you did not take stronger measures to bring Captain Kovacevic under your control in that interim period.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why I did not take any measures?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why you did not take stronger measures to keep Captain Kovacevic under your control during that time period.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the month of November, I asked for the removal of the commander of the brigade and the Chief of Staff. At that time, it was not established what the explicit guilt involved was in terms of the shelling of the Old Town in November. I did not have evidence to prove that this was done by Captain Kovacevic. But there were no orders for an investigation. There was no removal of the brigade command. And I did not have a free hand or orders to carry out an investigation and to request a removal of the commander of the battalion. What I established was not sufficient for me to act on my own in order to take measures against Captain Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say you did not have a free hand? Was there some element that interfered with your taking control or taking measures?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was not an order of the command or there was not a general feeling in favour of such an energetic measure or an independent investigation on my own. That's what I thought then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In favour where? Where was there not a general feeling?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the Superior Command. There has to be a general feeling. I mean, let me just add this -- to this, one more fact: In November --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript does not reflect when he speaks about the higher command. He said, "At the highest level," or something to that effect, at that level of the JNA. But it is not contained in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the month of November, if you remember, there was a letter written by General Kadijevic to the representative of the European Community, van Houten. In this letter it says that the JNA did not shell the town or the Old Town. I could not refute that by my own statements, or my own investigation, or the removal of Captain Kovacevic. Secondly, after that the 6th of December happened. The chief of the administration for information of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, General Milan Gvero, in the official statement claimed that Dubrovnik was not shelled and that no dust fell on the town. How can I now deny what the top brass of the General Staff is saying? And how can after that I remove the commander of the battalion and take independent measures on my own if no one ordered me to carry out a thorough investigation aimed at establishing the actual truth regarding the shelling of the Old Town? So at the level of the JNA, there was not a general feeling or determination, an intent to establish the truth, and my Superior Command did not order me to do anything in that direction either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you refer to your Superior Command, do you also include the 2nd Operational Group, or is that what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. General Strugar, as my superior officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you characterise the tone or the climate of the command of the 2nd Operational Group toward carrying out the investigations and putting into place measures which might be required following investigations into the shelling of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the command of the 2nd Operational Group certainly did not take any energetic action or issue orders in that direction aimed at even a superficial investigation, let alone a thorough and real one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the shelling of the 6th of December against the Old Town of Dubrovnik, why did you not attempt to have Captain Kovacevic removed or replaced?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not replace him because the commander of the 2nd Operational Group did not allow it. He protected him and said that he was a good lad. Those were his words. And that everything remained as it was. The battalion remained in place, and he remained in place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, Admiral Jokic, issue an order to shell the Old Town or to attack Srdj on the 6th of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anything that indicates to you that there may have been such an order in effect?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe that there is any room in the doctrine of the JNA and the regulations which -- for a battalion commander to initiate an attack without prior approval from his command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain the extent of planning and coordination that would be required for such an attack, such as took place on the 6th of December? And depending on your answer, would you be able to comment on whether or not the 6th of December attack went beyond the scale of a spontaneous counterattack?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that -- I mean, I did not quite understand your question. The proportion -- the scale of planning and attack?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me rephrase it for you, Admiral, so it's perfectly clear. Was there any evidence to you that might indicate that there may have been some prior planning behind the attack? And I would ask you to look at the extent of coordination of materiel, of weaponry that went into that attack, as well as the time period during which the attack continued, the duration of the attack. Do you understand my question now, Admiral? Is it consistent with a spontaneous reaction?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was not a spontaneous reaction. I knew it, then, too. But I did not know about all the preparations. As for the scale of preparations for such an attack, I think that at that level of battalion, it could have been carried out during the day, on the 5th, before the 6th of December. During the 5th of December, the battalion commander had to carry out preparations with his company commanders. Also, carry out agreement on acting in concert between certain parts of the battalion and preparing artillery fire for limited targeting of Srdj. So he did need several hours to carry out these preparations. And that shows that it was not a spontaneous attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Captain Kovacevic's movements on the eve before the attack?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Somers, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The evening before the attack, so you're clear, meaning the 5th of December.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I did not have any knowledge whatsoever. I know that he did not come to my command post on the 5th of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn anything subsequently about his movements?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, absolutely. As I investigated this, long after that, and that included all his company commanders, and when I talked to him, too, I established that he was carrying out preparations for an attack on the 5th of December and that he went to the command post of the 2nd Operational Group on the eve of the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was anything said about the events that were to take place on the 6th of December? Did anyone ask any questions as to why he was at the command post of the 2nd Operational Group as opposed to the command post of the unit to which he was subordinated, your command post?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wondered myself. I found that very surprising, that he went to the command post of the Superior Command, of my Superior Command, and without my knowledge, and I did not know of the intentions and objectives involved. Also, without reporting to me, or rather my command about going there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you indicate earlier that in notification of the units about the cease-fire that Captain Kovacevic himself did not appear? Or did he appear? Tell us, how was Captain Kovacevic's battalion made aware of the cease-fire arrangements on the 5th.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was informed by telephone from the forward command post of Kupari. He was informed in the afternoon on the 5th of December. He was informed by Captain Zec and Kozaric. One of the two of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who informed you that Captain Kovacevic visited the command post of the 2nd Operational Group on the eve of the 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told by two officers from the command of the 2nd Operational Group, and Rambo told me, or rather Captain Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About being present on the evening of the 5th of December.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did Captain Kovacevic, Rambo, confirm this to you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that to me before I went to The Hague. During a long conversation of several hours, I was questioning him. And I wanted to establish exactly what had happened on the 5th and 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself visit the command post of the 2nd Operational Group on the 5th of December? And if so, what time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as the talks at Cavtat ended, I went to Trebinje and informed General Strugar about the conclusion of the negotiations, about the fact that an agreement had been reached, that there was only one point that remained undefined, and that that was a pure formality. As for the rest, everything had been agreed upon. And a cease-fire order was supposed to be issued to all units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea what time Captain Kovacevic would have gone to the 2nd Operational Group on the 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He went after that time, sometime between 1700 hours and 1900 hours. Sometime between the two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to give us an idea of what time of day you had gone to the command post of the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometime between 1600 and 1700 hours, or rather between 1500 and 1600 hours. Sometime around then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was General Strugar present at the command post when you went?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally speak to General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you understand whether or not or did you know whether or not General Strugar moves about regularly when he's in Trebinje, or is he constantly -- I'm sorry. Does he move about regularly or is he constantly at his command post? What do you know about General Strugar's movements?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean on the 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In general.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot know at all where he was and what his movements were. He covered a broad range because his units were from Mostar to Dubrovnik, and he had Podgorica where he had to go, too. But I think that on the 6th of December, he was not at his command post. I think, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any high-level negotiations in which General Strugar may have played a part as commander of a 2nd Operational Group in 1992 in connection with issues settling Croatian territories?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know after I was relieved, he took part in negotiations with General Bobetko on a destroyer sometime in 1992. I don't know exactly which month. Zec told me about that, but I wasn't there then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the subject matter, if you know, if you were told, of the discussions? Did it concern Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these were talks, final talks, regarding the final withdrawal of units from the area of Dubrovnik on the basis of the Vance Plan that had been adopted in order to have the JNA withdraw from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you if you know of any protests that may have been lodged against the attack on the 6th of December and what your response was to those protests?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As for me, not to repeat everything that I've already said, I said to Minister Davorin and in the fax that I sent to Dubrovnik, I expressed my regrets over what had happened and so on. The protest, the official protest, went to the command of the 2nd Operational Group. I don't know exactly what General Strugar's response was. I know what he said to me, but I don't know officially what his response was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask you, please, to turn to tab 39 in your binders.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry. I'm corrected. I have 39. It should be 34.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, looking at this document, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's dated 6 December 1991, and it reflects a fax time of 15.36, but it says at the bottom, "Received at approximately 1400." And who is it to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was addressed to the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik, or rather, Minister Davorin Rudolf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please just very quickly read the first lines of the message.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what it says, "These talks would be issued, continue tomorrow, 12.00 after my return from Belgrade" --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you're not -- under message, where it says, "Your Excellency," at the very beginning of your message.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read that, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I express my sincere regret for the difficult and unfortunate situation that has been created. This was not our order, neither was it ever in my mind to act this way. General Kadijevic sent a message to you and to the ECMM in Dubrovnik on undertaking an energetic investigation at our responsibility and the guilty ones for this event. At the same time, we expect responsibility to be established on your side, too, for the sake of a thorough clarification of all circumstances with regard to the events from last night and this morning."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask to move this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is P136.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving quickly to tab 39, please. Admiral Jokic, in front of you is a document. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a directive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the date of the directive, Admiral?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 10th of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is it from, this directive?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a directive of the Federal Secretary for National Defence on the use of armed forces in the coming period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to turn your attention to paragraph 6, please, under -- where it says, "Zadatke." If you could just let us know, what does paragraph 6 say?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The paragraph says, "In all areas of combat activity, place in command the most senior officer of the JNA all units of the JNA and TO, as well as volunteer units which agreed to be subordinate to that command and wear JNA and TO insignia. All other armed formations should consider to be paramilitaries and should be disarmed and removed from the zone of combat activities. Take all steps to prevent looting and genocidal, vengeful behaviour. To this end, establish necessary control by engaging military police organs and units designated for that purpose as well as criminal prosecution organs."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Admiral. Now, this was issued after the attack on the 6th of December. Do you know why?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably because previous orders were not obeyed in respect of command and using different units, diverse units, including volunteers and paramilitary units that probably did exist in certain areas. Also, in terms of this vengeful behaviour and looting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd ask to move this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is numbered P137.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, you have discussed your having come to The Hague. And I want to ask you if you were charged by the Office of the Prosecutor with violations of the laws or customs of war relating the shelling of the Old Town of Dubrovnik on 6 December 1991. Were you charged with violations? Were you indicted? Was there an indictment against you for the attacks, your role in the attacks against the Old Town of Dubrovnik on 6 December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the counts indicate -- I'm sorry. Did the counts include murder, cruel treatment, unlawful attack on civilians, devastation not justified by military necessity, unlawful attack on civilian objects, destruction or wilful damage done to institutions dedicated to religion, charity, and education, the arts and sciences, historic monuments and works of art and science?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these the same counts that General Strugar is charged with? Same charges?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you enter a plea of guilty to all counts before another Trial Chamber of this institution on the 27th of August 2003?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you sentenced to a period of seven years' incarceration on the 18th of March 2004?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you currently in the Detention Unit of the United Nations prior to any further action on that imposition of sentence?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as a final point, there is a video that has some reference to the individuals that Admiral Jokic has mentioned tour the Old Town on behalf of the JNA. I fear because of time the most I could try to do would be to show the video enough to identify it - I'm proffering what I would do - and then seek admission. And whatever weight the Chamber wishes to affix to it, simply leave in your hands. But I think time would prohibit anything more than that. If that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is the playing time?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I believe it's over 20 minutes. And I think that would be not appropriate to have the Chamber wait beyond this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The timing at the moment, we would be delaying the cross-examination of Admiral Jokic until after the evidence of -- or the completion of the evidence of the Ambassador. I wonder whether you would want to finalise dealing with that tape at the commencement of the next session of the Admiral's evidence. In other words, not close your case now; deal with it when the Admiral resumes as the one last thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We could do that. The Defence was given this video. It had not been on the original exhibit list. It was given prior to the commencement of testimony. And I hope that has offered enough time to review it without any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What I propose will give them even further time. I know that Mr. Petrovic was anxious to say something. He might say it at the resumption of evidence of the Admiral.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What we might do is interrupt at this point the evidence of Admiral Jokic for him to return certainly not tomorrow, but probably the day following. And we will hear any submissions there may be tomorrow about the resumption date of Admiral Jokic's evidence. We will -- on the resumption of his evidence, whenever that is, you will deal with that tape and any submissions of the Defence. Now, is it still proposed that the Ambassador will give evidence tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. The Ambassador is actually here today, but I believe the time is not favourable to starting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It would be impractical, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What we will do is adjourn for today, resume tomorrow morning. At the resumption tomorrow morning, we would hear brief submissions on the way the Tribunal should deal with the medical condition of the accused; that is, whether it should be dealt with on the written record or whether we should hear oral evidence. We will hear those submissions tomorrow morning. They need only be brief. And we will then hear the Ambassador, and we will then hear any submissions that are to be made about the resumption date and time of the evidence of the Admiral. At the moment, we would anticipate that could be Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I just bring to the Chamber's attention that from the binder, there were several tabs from which we did not draw, so you know. I think tab 40 is already in evidence, if I'm not wrong. But I didn't refer to it here. Tabs 35, 36 were not tendered. 40 and 36 -- I'm sorry, I have that backward. 40 and 36 were not tendered. 35 is in evidence.
